newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam set to issue Brady bonds at end of June.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam set to issue Brady bonds at end of June.

text.p: Vietnam is likely to issue Brady bonds at the end of June as part of a deal to restructure its foreign bank debt, the co-chairman of the country's Bank Advisory Committee said on Thursday.

"Everything is on schedule for basically the end of June at this stage," Rollo Prendergast, regional head for Global Structured Finance at ANZ Bank in Hong Kong, told Reuters by phone. "There is nothing that we are aware of that should get in the way of that original timetable, which was...agreed with the Vietnamese side back in December."

Officials at the central State Bank of Vietnam declined to comment immediately on the planned bond issue, which was agreed almost a year ago as part of a debt reastructuring deal which Hanoi hammered out with its creditors.

At that time, the debt was put at around $900 million. However, Prendergast said that since the bulk of the debt was in German marks, the dollar's subsequent rise may have reduced the total to nearer $700 million.

Under the framework agreement -- which Prendergast said had been accepted by creditors representing around 90 percent of the total owed -- creditors have a choice of recovering principal through a 50-percent discount bond or a par bond.
Both bonds will be backed by 30-year U.S. Treasury zero coupon bonds bought by Vietnam.
Prendergast said the question of the U.S. treasury bonds was discussed when U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin visited Vietnam earlier this month.
Analysts say the deal, a signal of Vietnam's willingness to repay its debts, would open the way for the country to tap the international financial markets.
Moody's Investors Service put the prospect of a debut Vietnam Eurobond back in the spotlight last week when it rated the country's sovereign debt.
The agency assigned a Ba3 rating to long-term foreign-currency bonds and notes of issuers domiciled in Vietnam and said it expected to assign the same rating to a eurobond.

Vietnam last year mandated Merrill Lynch and Nomura Securities to arrange the bond, though it was urged by the World Bank to delay the launch until it had reached full agreement with its foreign commercial creditors on defaulted loans.
Market sources said they expected Vietnam's first eurobond would probably total between $100 million and $150 million, with a maturity of either three or five years.
